summary: Adds two optional features to TWAMP. One lets the responding host return some of the command or padding octets to the sender, and the other makes test packets the same size in both directions.

plainLanguage.summary: TWAMP measures a path by sending test packets and timing the replies. This document adds two optional features: one that lets the sending host put a few bytes of its own choosing into the test packet and get them back in the reply, and one that guarantees the reply packet is exactly the same size as the packet sent, so a size difference never confuses the measurement.

subtitle: Two optional TWAMP add-ons: bounce chosen bytes back to the sender, and keep test packets the same size in both directions.

tldr.problem: Core TWAMP lets the reflector shrink its reply by truncating padding, but that is not guaranteed and is impossible when there is too little padding. Senders also have no assured way to tag a packet and get the tag back.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns two new bits in the TWAMP Modes field. Reflect Octets makes the Server and Session-Reflector return designated octets, and Symmetrical Size defines a new Session-Sender packet format that already has the reflector's larger header built in.
tldr.outcome: Both features are OPTIONAL, and a system does not need them to claim compliance with RFC 5357. The RFC updates RFC 5357 and says the extensions do not appear to permit any new attacks.

today: RFC 6038 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010 that updates RFC 5357. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Optional Extensions
sections.content:
The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol of RFC 5357 is an extension of the One-way Active Measurement Protocol of RFC 4656. The TWAMP specification gathered wide review as it approached completion, and the by-products were several recommendations for new features in TWAMP, which this memo describes.

One feature is the OPTIONAL capability for the responder host to return a limited number of unassigned, that is padding, octets to the Control-Client or Session-Sender entities in both the TWAMP-Control and TWAMP-Test protocols. With this capability, the Control-Client or Session-Sender can embed octets of information it deems useful and have the assurance that the corresponding reply or test packet will contain that information when it is reflected and returned by the Server or Session-Reflector.

The memo also adds an OPTIONAL capability to ensure that reflected test packets are the same size in both directions of transmission, accomplished by specifying a new TWAMP-Test Session-Sender packet format. Although TWAMP recommends padding truncation to achieve symmetrical sizes, to compensate for the Session-Reflector's larger test packet header, it is not guaranteed that the Session-Reflector will truncate the padding, and it is not possible if there is insufficient padding.

This memo is an update to the TWAMP core protocol of RFC 5357. Measurement systems are not required to implement the features described here to claim compliance with RFC 5357. Throughout the memo, bits marked MBZ, Must Be Zero, MUST be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers, and the HMAC MUST be calculated as defined in Section 3.2 of RFC 4656.
sections.plainLanguage: Both features are optional, and a measurement system that ignores them is still a conforming TWAMP system. The first one lets a sender mark a packet and get the mark back; the second makes the reply packet exactly the same size as the one that was sent.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The purpose of the memo is to define two closely related OPTIONAL features for TWAMP. The features enhance the TWAMP host's capabilities to perform a simple operation on control and test packets: the reflection of octets or padding, and the capability to ensure symmetrical size TWAMP-Test packets. Motivations include permitting the controller host to tag packets with an index for simplified identification, and asserting that the same size test packets will be used in each direction.

The scope is limited to two features. Reflect Octets is the capability of the Server and Session-Reflector to reflect specific octets back to the Client and Session-Sender, and the similar service provided by the Client and Session-Sender. Symmetrical Size is the capability to ensure that the TWAMP-Test protocol uses the same packet size in both directions, through support of a new TWAMP-Test Session-Sender test packet format in both the Session-Sender and the Session-Reflector; only the Session-Sender test packet format is new.

The memo extends the modes of operation through the assignment of two new values in the Modes field, while retaining backward compatibility with the core TWAMP implementations. The two new values correspond to the two features. When the Server and the Control-Client have agreed to use the Reflect Octets mode during control connection setup, the Control-Client, the Server, the Session-Sender and the Session-Reflector MUST all conform to the requirements of that mode, and the same applies to the Symmetrical Size mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Both features are negotiated once, on the control connection, and then every session set up under it follows the same rules. The two are close enough to be defined together, because the second changes how much padding there is and the first uses padding to carry information.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use the Features
sections.content:
TWAMP connection establishment follows the procedure defined in Section 3.1 of RFC 4656 and Section 3.1 of RFC 5357. The new features need two new bit positions, and their values, to identify the ability of the Server and Session-Reflector to reflect specific octets back to the Control-Client and Session-Sender, and to support the new Session-Sender packet format in the TWAMP-Test protocol.

The Server sets one or both of the new bit positions in the Modes field of the Server Greeting message to indicate its capabilities and willingness to operate in either of these modes, or both. If the Control-Client intends to operate all test sessions invoked with this control connection using one or both of the new modes, it MUST set the Mode field bit corresponding to each function in the Setup Response message. With this and other extensions, the Control-Client MAY set multiple Mode field bits in the Setup Response message.

The value of the Modes field sent by the Server in the Server Greeting message is the bit-wise OR of the mode values that it is willing to support during this session. With the publication of this memo as an RFC, the last 7 bit positions of the 32-bit Modes field are used. A Control-Client conforming to this extension MAY ignore the values in the higher bits of the Modes field, or it MAY support other features communicated in those bit positions, and the other bits remain available for future protocol extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The Server says in its greeting which of the two features it can do, and the Control-Client answers with the ones it wants to use. The choice is made once for the whole control connection, so every session started on it behaves the same way.

sections.title: The Reflect Octets Control Packets
sections.content:
In the Request-TW-Session command, the Reflect Octets feature adds two fields after the Type-P Descriptor. The Octets to be reflected field is 2 octets long and contains the octets that the Server MUST reflect in the Accept Session message. The Length of padding to reflect field is 2 octets long and holds an unsigned binary value in units of octets. It communicates the length of the padding in the TWAMP-Test packet that the Session-Sender expects to be reflected, and the length of octets the Session-Reflector SHALL return in its TWAMP-Test packet format. By including the length in the Request-TW-Session message, a Server is able to determine whether it can comply with a specific request to reflect padding, and to arrange for the Session-Reflector processing in advance.

The Padding Length field continues to specify the number of padding octets that the Session-Sender will append to all TWAMP-Test packets associated with the test session. It SHOULD be at least 27 octets in Unauthenticated TWAMP-Test mode, and at least 56 octets in the Authenticated or Encrypted modes, to allow for the truncation process that TWAMP recommends. It SHALL be greater than the Length of padding to reflect when using the OPTIONAL Reflect Octets mode. In Unauthenticated mode it SHALL be at least 27 plus the Length of padding to reflect octets when using both the Reflect Octets mode and the truncation process, and in Authenticated or Encrypted modes at least 56 plus that length.

In the Accept Session command, the Reflected octets field contains the octets from the Request-TW-Session Octets to be reflected field and is 2 octets long. The Server octets field contains information that the Server intends to be returned in the TWAMP-Test packet padding, or SHALL be zero, and is 2 octets long. Compliant implementations using the Reflect Octets feature MUST send all zeros in the Server octets field when the Server does not require octets to be returned in test packets, MUST send a non-zero value when it does, and in that case the TWAMP-Test Sender MUST include those octets at the beginning of the padding field. When performing the truncation process, if the padding calculations show there are insufficient octets to produce equal-length test packets, the Accept field MUST be set to 3 to indicate that some aspect of the request is not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The session request carries two bytes the sender wants back, and a number saying how much padding should come back with them. The answer carries the two bytes echoed, plus two bytes of the Server's own that it wants reflected in the test packets. The padding has to be long enough for the feature to work, and if it is not, the Server refuses the session.

sections.title: Padding, Truncation and the Reflector's Reply
sections.content:
In Reflect Octets mode the original TWAMP-Test packet padding field is re-designated as the padding to be reflected, and its length corresponds to the Length of padding to reflect field of the Request-TW-Session command. Those are the octets the Session-Sender expects back from the Session-Reflector. The length of the additional padding is the difference between the Padding Length and the Length of padding to reflect. When the Server intends octets to be returned in test packets, the Session-Sender MUST include them in the first 2 octets of the padding to be reflected field, and the Session-Reflector MUST reflect those octets as it does the rest of that field.

When the Reflect Octets mode is selected and the truncation process that TWAMP recommends is used, the Session-Sender MUST anticipate the minimum padding needed to achieve equal-size test packets in both directions, and that amount depends on the security mode and on whether Reflect Octets is selected at the same time. With the truncation process alone, the Session-Sender MUST append sufficient padding to allow the same IP packet payload lengths in each direction, and to compensate for the Session-Reflector's larger test packet format it MUST append at least 27 octets of padding in Unauthenticated mode and at least 56 octets in Authenticated and Encrypted modes. The document tabulates the sizes: the reflector header is 41 octets in Unauthenticated mode and 104 in Authenticated or Encrypted mode, the sender header is 14 and 48 octets, and the truncated padding is 27 and 56 octets.

With Reflect Octets selected at the same time, the Session-Sender MUST append at least 27 octets of padding plus the Length of padding to reflect in Unauthenticated mode, and at least 56 octets plus that length in Authenticated and Encrypted modes.

On the reflector side, the designated octets in the padding field of the Session-Sender's test packet MUST be included in the Session-Reflector's test packet. The padding from the Session-Sender field in the reflector's packet MUST be the same octets as the padding to be reflected field of the sender's packet, and so MUST conform to the length specified in the Request-TW-Session message. When the Server returned a non-zero Server octets field, the Session-Reflector SHALL reflect those octets as well. When using the recommended truncation process together with Reflect Octets, the Session-Reflector MUST reflect the designated octets and MAY reuse additional padding from the Session-Sender, and it MUST truncate the padding so that the highest-numbered octets are discarded and the test packet length equals the Session-Sender's packet length, which means truncating exactly 27 octets in Unauthenticated mode and exactly 56 octets in Authenticated and Encrypted modes.
sections.plainLanguage: The reflector's reply has a bigger header than the sender's packet, so it trims padding to make up the difference. With the reflect feature in use, the padding it trims is the part the sender did not ask to have returned, and the numbers say how much padding the sender must add so there is always enough to trim.

sections.title: The New Session-Sender Packet Format
sections.content:
When the Symmetrical Size mode is selected, the Session-Sender SHALL use a new TWAMP-Test packet format in Unauthenticated mode. The packet keeps the sequence number, the timestamp and the error estimate, and then carries 27 octets that must be zero before the packet padding begins. The padding octets are separated from the information fields, which is what allows the two directions to end up the same size.

This feature requires only a new Session-Sender test packet format; the Session-Reflector test packet format is unchanged.

When both the Symmetrical Size mode and the Reflect Octets mode are selected, the Session-Sender uses the same format with the padding to be reflected following the 27 must-be-zero octets, followed by the additional packet padding. In Authenticated or Encrypted modes the padding to be reflected follows 56 must-be-zero octets instead.

On the reflector side, when Symmetrical Size mode is selected, the Session-Reflector packet formats for Unauthenticated and Authenticated or Encrypted modes are identical to the core TWAMP specification, so the reflector's format is unchanged. The Session-Reflector MUST construct its test packet using the information in the Session-Sender's test packet, and the length of the reflector's test packet SHALL equal the length of the sender's test packet. When both modes are selected, the Session-Reflector MUST operate using the Session-Sender packet format with the padding octets separated from the information fields and the padding to be reflected preceding the additional padding, and it SHALL use the same packet format as the Reflect Octets case.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of hoping the reflector trims its padding, the sender builds a packet that already has room for the reflector's bigger header. The result is that the reply packet comes back exactly the same length as the one that was sent, with no reliance on the reflector doing anything special.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: These extended modes of operation do not appear to permit any new attacks on hosts communicating with core TWAMP. The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks are relevant here as well, and the reader is referred to RFC 4656 and RFC 5357.
sections.plainLanguage: The document finds no new attack surface in either feature. The usual cautions about running active measurements on a live network still apply.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The memo adds two modes to the IANA registry for the TWAMP Modes field, and describes the behavior when the new modes are used. The field is a recognized extension mechanism for TWAMP. IANA has created a TWAMP-Modes registry, as requested in RFC 5618. The modes are specified in TWAMP Server Greeting and Setup Response messages, and are indicated by setting bits in the 32-bit Modes field that correspond to values in the registry. New features are expected to be assigned increasing registry values that correspond to single bit positions, unless there is a good reason not to.

The registry is augmented with two values. Value 32 is Reflect Octets Capability, a new bit position, number 5. Value 64 is Symmetrical Size Sender Test Packet Format, a new bit position, number 6.
sections.plainLanguage: Each feature gets one bit in the Modes field: bit 5 for reflecting octets and bit 6 for the symmetrical size format. The rest of the field is left for future extensions.
